after: ## What patterns does recorded crime show?
alt: A funnel narrowing from all crime committed, to crime reported, to crime recorded, to arrests and convictions. At each step crime drops out: much is never reported, some reports are not recorded, and policing decides who is targeted and caught.
caption: Official statistics show who gets caught, which is not the same as who offends.

after: ## Why do young people appear more criminal? (6.2.2)
alt: Six explanations around the fact that young people are over-represented in recorded crime: police targeting, stereotyping and the self-fulfilling prophecy, gang culture, weaker social control, lack of opportunity, and status frustration (Albert Cohen, 1955).
caption: Some explanations concern how youth are policed; others concern why some young people offend.

after: ## Why do men commit more crime than women? (6.2.4)
alt: Two columns. Factors pushing men’s crime up: a culture of masculinity, Miller’s focal concerns and misogyny. Factors keeping women’s recorded crime down: closer supervision of girls, Pollak’s chivalry thesis, and Carlen’s finding that women offended when the rewards of conformity failed.
caption: The gender gap comes from what drives men’s offending and what restrains or hides women’s.

after: ## What do the main theories say? (6.2.6)
alt: Two chains of three steps. Labelling (Becker, 1963): an act is labelled deviant, others react to the person as deviant, and a deviant career can follow. Moral panic (Stanley Cohen, 1972): the media exaggerate a group’s behaviour, the group become folk devils, and tougher control follows.
caption: Interactionists focus on how reactions to deviance can create more of it.

alt: A table of five theories. Strain and subculture fit property crime by young working-class men but not corporate crime; labelling fits how reactions shape careers but not the first act; Marxism fits crimes of the powerful but can neglect victims; feminism fits gender patterns but may treat women as one group; postmodernism fits new crimes but offers no single cause.
caption: Each theory fits some crimes well and others poorly.

after: ## What are the aims of punishment? (6.3.1)
alt: Five cards for the aims of punishment: protection, deterrence (individual and general), retribution, incapacitation and rehabilitation. Below, prison is shown as incapacitating and seen as just but with high reoffending, while Norway’s Halden prison stresses rehabilitation.
caption: Judge a punishment by which aims it meets and which it misses.

alt: Cards weighing policing strategies. Stop and search detects weapons and drugs but may damage trust; surveillance helps detection but raises privacy concerns and may displace crime; community policing builds trust; military-style policing may restore order quickly but can alienate communities. Crime prevention includes street lighting, housing design and youth programmes.
caption: Every policing strategy trades effectiveness against trust, privacy or consent.
